newsitem.title: USA: UPS strike seen delivering light blow to US growth.
newsitem.headline: UPS strike seen delivering light blow to US growth.

text.p: Strikers at United Parcel Service, the world's largest parcel delivery company, could dampen the nation's economic growth in the third quarter.
Complicating deliveries for major retailers around the country, the nationwide Teamsters strike was expected to cause disruptions to inventory building and sales over the next month.
Companies that relied on UPS's handling some 12 million packages a day have sought other alternatives to receive their goods amid a traffic bottleneck analysts said.
In the wake of the strike, delivery times have already slowed, analysts said.
William Griggs, managing director at Griggs & Santow Inc, said the strike would probably distort the behavior of the economy in the near term, mostly in the retail sector.
"My wife owns a book store and a lot of the books come through UPS," he said. "Now, she has to rely on someone else who may not be able to handle the capacity."
Some companies such as Seattle-based Amazon.com Inc, the leading online retailer of books, were able to prepare for such delivery disruptions.
"Our operations team prepared for the eventuality of the UPS strike, and transitioned any UPS shipments to the U.S. (Postal Service) and Airborne" Express, said a company spokeswoman.
But smaller firms, like Momeni Inc, a family owned import rug wholesale business in New York, faced mounting problems.
Ali Momeni, vice president of production and merchandising, said his company used UPS for over 50 percent of its shipments. He said other delivery service companies were backed up.
"UPS is impacting our business because we can't ship to our customers. Our inventory builds up and we can't invoice customers," he said.
Some analysts estimated the strike could shave a tenth of a percentage point off Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in the third quarter.
However, as long as the strike is short-lived, its negative impact on the nation's GDP should be swift and modest, they said.

Analysts said modest effects from the strike could show up in economic reports, including employment numbers and the National Association of Puchasing Management (NAPM) index of manufacturing activity.
"We see some spikes to the monthly information if the strike continues," said Kurt Karl, chief economist at WEFA Inc's U.S. forecasting center.
He said employment could be off about 200,000, and the NAPM's delivery index might get "severely retarded."
But Karl said the timing of the strike takes away some of its sting.
"The good news for the economy and the industry is that this is a fairly lax time of the year for on-time delveries -- it's not like a big shopping holiday period," he said.
